title: Which spot wins every vote?
hook: Five voters on a left-right line. Which spot can beat every rival head-to-head?

doesNotKnow: that with single-peaked preferences the median voter's favourite beats every rival in a two-way vote

misconception: The position that wins every head-to-head vote is the average voter's position.
objective: The learner can explain that a two-way vote splits the voters at the halfway point between the two positions, so the middle voter (at 3) is always on the winning side of 3; with favourites 1, 2, 3, 8 and 10 the average 4.8 loses to 4 and the centre 5 loses to 3, while 3 beats every rival.

claims.text: With favourites at 1, 2, 3, 8 and 10, position 3 beats every other whole-number position from 0 to 10 in a two-way majority vote, and it is the only one that does.
claims.source: Builder's node pairwise check, 2026-10-14 (each voter votes for the nearer position, equidistant voters abstain): whole-number positions beat 4, 6, 8, 10, 8, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 of the other 10 for positions 0..10; only 3 beats all 10. Same duel() as Demo.tsx, which draws the strip. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node copy of duel(): wins vs other whole numbers 4,6,8,10,8,6,4,3,2,1,0 for 0..10; only 3 beats all 10. On a 0.1 grid too, only 3 beats every other position.

claims.text: The average of the favourites is 4.8, and 3 beats 5 by 3 votes to 2.
claims.source: (1 + 2 + 3 + 8 + 10) / 5 = 24 / 5 = 4.8. Against 5 the halfway point is 4: voters 1, 2, 3 are nearer 3, voters 8 and 10 nearer 5. Re-run in node 2026-10-14. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): 24/5 = 4.8; duel(3,5) = 3-2 (own node). Reveal states only that 5 lost; the stage shows 3-2.

claims.text: A rival at 4 beats the average, 4.8, by 3 votes to 2: voters 1, 2 and 3 are nearer 4. Any rival that beats 4.8 wins exactly voters 1, 2 and 3.
claims.source: Halfway point 4.4; voters 1, 2, 3 lie below it, 8 and 10 above. node duel(40, 48) = [3, 2] for 4, 2026-10-14. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): duel(4,4.8) = 3-2, halfway 4.4 (own node); matches the reveal. | REVISED v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): v2 reveal quotes the rival position the learner saw 4.8 lose to (recorded; the rival starts at 4) and lists the nearer voters computed by Demo.tsx nearerVoters; added the general statement that a rival beating 4.8 always wins exactly voters 1, 2, 3 (a rival right of 4.8 can win at most 8 and 10; a rival left of 4.8 wins voters below the halfway point, and needs 3 of them). Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own duel() brute force over every rival 0.0-10.0 in tenths: rival 4 vs 4.8 is 3-2 (voters 1, 2, 3); every rival that beats 4.8 wins exactly {1, 2, 3}.

claims.text: Any rival to the right of 3 loses voters 1, 2 and 3 to position 3, and any rival to the left loses voters 3, 8 and 10, so the middle voter is on the winning side of every split.
claims.source: For a rival r > 3 the halfway point (3 + r) / 2 is above 3, so voters at 1, 2, 3 are strictly nearer 3; for r < 3 the halfway point is below 3, so voters at 3, 8, 10 are nearer 3. Three of five is a majority. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node check over every rival 0..10 in tenths: r>3 keeps 1,2,3 strictly nearer 3; r<3 keeps 3,8,10. 3 of 5 is a majority.

claims.text: The average is pulled by how far away 8 and 10 sit, while a two-way vote only asks which side of the halfway point each voter is on.
claims.source: The mean depends on the values (moving 10 to 100 moves it), while the vote count depends only on each voter's side of (a + b) / 2, i.e. on order. Definition-level argument. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Definition-level: the vote count depends only on each voter's side of (a+b)/2; the mean depends on values. Correct.

claims.text: When each voter prefers positions nearer their favourite (single-peaked preferences), the median voter's favourite beats every rival in a two-way majority vote (median voter theorem).
claims.source: Easley & Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 23; D. Black, 'On the Rationale of Group Decision-making', J. Political Economy 56 (1948). Citation from the brief; attribution for the fact-checker to confirm. Stated for an odd number of voters; the lesson has five. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Verified on derivation (c4 argument holds for any odd number of voters with single-peaked preferences). Black 1948, JPE 56(1) correct to my knowledge and confirmed as the origin by web search snippets (paper not opened). E&K ch. 23 'Voting' (sec. 23.6 median voter theorem) from my own knowledge, not confirmed (book host blocked); high confidence.

claims.text: A rival at 4 beats the centre, 5, by 3 votes to 2.
claims.source: Halfway point between 4 and 5 is 4.5; voters 1, 2 and 3 are nearer 4, voters 8 and 10 nearer 5: 3-2. Demo.tsx duel(50, 40) gives [2, 3]. Reveal: 'The centre, 5, lost too, to the rival at 4' (rival position quoted from the learner's recorded duel). Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own duel(50, 40): 2-3, rival wins with voters 1, 2, 3 (halfway 4.5). Rival starts at 4, so the first 5 test shows it.

recall.question: Seven voters' favourites sit at 0, 1, 2, 4, 9, 9 and 10 on a line; each prefers nearer. Which position beats every rival one-on-one?
recall.why: 4 is the middle (fourth) favourite. Any rival to its right loses the four voters at 0, 1, 2 and 4; any to its left loses 4, 9, 9 and 10. The average, 5, does not matter.
